advances:
This proves the exact registered near-heavy-line lemma. It constructs one
compatible rank-zero or rank-one affine fiber-depth certificate on the line,
including the factor \(2^{-q(E)}\). If the line mass is at least \(eW/6\),
the certificate has value at least \(W/64\). In rank zero this is transferred
to ambient mixed depth directly; in rank one it is transferred through the
primitive lattice coordinate and accepted fact `b220933817d23295`.

Thus any remaining counterexample to the open global affine-capacity subgoal
must have every primitive affine lattice line of mass strictly less than
\(eW/6\). This auxiliary lemma does not prove that global subgoal when all
line masses are below this threshold and does not close the locked target.

proof:
We first record the comparison between fiber mass and maximal fiber depth.
Fix \(z\) with \(w_z>0\), and let \(\rho_z\) be the finite measure on
\(\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^d\) given by
\[
\rho_z:=\delta_0\otimes
\left(\operatorname{Leb}_d\mathbin{\restriction}C_z\right).
\tag{8}
\]
This is a nonzero compactly supported log-concave measure. Its base marginal
is \(w_z\delta_0\), so every closed base halfspace containing \(0\) has
mass \(w_z\). Apply accepted fact `f049539ffd9c9b1d` with base dimension
one, \(z_0=0\), and \(\alpha=1\). The selected submeasure has the same
total mass as \(\rho_z\) and is dominated by \(\rho_z\), hence it equals
\(\rho_z\). The accepted fact therefore gives a point
\((0,x_z)\), with \(x_z\in C_z\), such that every closed ambient halfspace
containing \((0,x_z)\) has \(\rho_z\)-mass at least \(w_z/e\).

For every proper closed halfspace \(J\subseteq\mathbb R^d\) containing
\(x_z\), the product halfspace \(\mathbb R\times J\) contains
\((0,x_z)\) and has \(\rho_z\)-mass
\(\operatorname{vol}_d(C_z\cap J)\). Hence
\[
\delta_z(x_z)\geq\frac{w_z}{e},
\qquad
M_z\geq\frac{w_z}{e}.
\tag{9}
\]
Attainment of the maximum in (3) also follows from accepted fact
`4e868f774de77608`.

We next prove the finite concave-sequence lemma used to choose a chord. Let
\[
r_0\geq r_1\geq\cdots\geq r_m\geq0
\tag{10}
\]
be a finite sequence whose drops
\[
\Delta_k:=r_{k-1}-r_k
\qquad(1\leq k\leq m)
\tag{11}
\]
are nondecreasing. For \(j\geq1\), define
\[
B_j:=
\sum_{k=0}^j
\left(
\left(1-\frac{k}{j}\right)r_0+\frac{k}{j}r_j
\right)^d,
\qquad
B_0:=r_0^d.
\tag{12}
\]
We claim that some \(j\in\{0,\ldots,m\}\) satisfies
\[
B_j\geq\frac38\sum_{k=0}^m r_k^d.
\tag{13}
\]

If \(r_0=0\), then every term of the sequence is zero, and \(j=0\) proves
(13). Hence assume \(r_0>0\). Put
\[
\vartheta:=\frac d{d+1},\qquad
\gamma:=\vartheta^d,\qquad
\eta:=\vartheta^{d+1}.
\tag{14}
\]
The binomial theorem gives
\[
\left(1+\frac1d\right)^d\geq2
\quad\text{and}\quad
\left(1+\frac1d\right)^{d+1}
\geq
1+\frac{d+1}{d}
+\binom{d+1}{2}\frac1{d^2}
=\frac52+\frac{3}{2d}>\frac52.
\]
Therefore
\[
\gamma\leq\frac12,\qquad \eta<\frac25.
\tag{15}
\]

First suppose
\[
r_k\geq\vartheta r_0
\qquad(0\leq k\leq m).
\tag{16}
\]
If \(m=0\), choose \(j=0\). If \(m\geq1\), choose \(j=m\). The chord
joining \(r_0\) to \(r_m\) is bounded below at its \(k\)-th lattice point
by
\[
r_0\left(1-\frac{k}{m(d+1)}\right).
\tag{17}
\]
The function
\[
\phi(x):=\left(1-\frac{x}{d+1}\right)^d
\qquad(0\leq x\leq1)
\]
is convex. The composite trapezoidal inequality therefore gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
B_m
&\geq r_0^d\sum_{k=0}^m\phi(k/m)\\
&\geq r_0^d\left[
m\int_0^1\phi(x)\,dx+\frac{\phi(0)+\phi(1)}2
\right]\\
&=r_0^d\left[
m(1-\eta)+\frac{1+\gamma}{2}
\right].
\end{aligned}
\tag{18}
\]
Since
\[
\sum_{k=0}^m r_k^d\leq(m+1)r_0^d,
\tag{19}
\]
equations (15), (18), and (19) imply
\[
8B_m-3\sum_{k=0}^m r_k^d
\geq
r_0^d\left[m(5-8\eta)+1+4\gamma\right]>0.
\tag{20}
\]
This proves (13) in the first case.

Suppose (16) fails, and let
\[
j:=\max\{k:r_k\geq\vartheta r_0\}.
\tag{21}
\]
Then \(j<m\) and
\[
r_{j+1}<\vartheta r_0.
\tag{22}
\]
If \(j=0\), then
\[
\Delta_1>\frac{r_0}{d+1}.
\]
Since the drops are nondecreasing, for \(1\leq k\leq m\),
\[
r_k<
r_0\left(1-\frac{k}{d+1}\right).
\tag{23}
\]
Nonnegativity forces \(m\leq d\). Thus
\[
\begin{aligned}
\sum_{k=0}^m r_k^d
&<
r_0^d\sum_{k=0}^{d}
\left(1-\frac{k}{d+1}\right)^d\\
&=
r_0^d\sum_{h=1}^{d+1}
\left(\frac{h}{d+1}\right)^d
\leq2r_0^d.
\end{aligned}
\tag{24}
\]
For the last inequality, the summand is nondecreasing in \(h\), so the sum
excluding its last term is at most the integral of
\((x/(d+1))^d\) over \([0,d+1]\), which equals \(1\), while the last term
equals \(1\). Hence \(B_0=r_0^d\) is more than one half of the total in
(24), and (13) follows.

It remains to treat \(j\geq1\). Put
\[
h:=\frac{r_0}{(d+1)(j+1)}.
\tag{25}
\]
The average of the first \(j+1\) drops and (22) give
\[
\Delta_{j+1}
\geq\frac{r_0-r_{j+1}}{j+1}>h.
\tag{26}
\]
Every subsequent drop is at least \(\Delta_{j+1}\). Consequently, for
\(0\leq l\leq m-j-1\),
\[
r_{j+1+l}
\leq\left(\vartheta r_0-lh\right)_+.
\tag{27}
\]
The right-hand side of (27), raised to the \(d\)-th power, is
nonincreasing in \(l\). Its sum over nonnegative integers is at most its
initial value plus its integral, so
\[
\begin{aligned}
\sum_{k=j+1}^m r_k^d
&\leq
\gamma r_0^d+
\int_0^\infty(\vartheta r_0-hx)_+^d\,dx\\
&=
\left[\gamma+\eta(j+1)\right]r_0^d.
\end{aligned}
\tag{28}
\]
Adding the trivial bound on the prefix yields
\[
\sum_{k=0}^m r_k^d
\leq
\left[(j+1)(1+\eta)+\gamma\right]r_0^d.
\tag{29}
\]
On the other hand, \(r_j\geq\vartheta r_0\), so the same trapezoidal
estimate as in (18) gives
\[
B_j\geq
r_0^d\left[
j(1-\eta)+\frac{1+\gamma}{2}
\right].
\tag{30}
\]
Equations (29) and (30) imply
\[
8B_j-3\sum_{k=0}^m r_k^d
\geq
r_0^d\left[
j(5-11\eta)+1+\gamma-3\eta
\right].
\tag{31}
\]
Here \(5-11\eta>5-22/5>0\). Also, since
\(\eta=\vartheta\gamma\), \(\vartheta<1\), and \(\gamma\leq1/2\),
\[
1+\gamma-3\eta
=1-\gamma(3\vartheta-1)
>1-2\gamma\geq0.
\tag{32}
\]
Thus the right-hand side of (31) is positive. This completes the proof of
the sequence lemma, including the all-zero sequence.

We now apply the sequence lemma to \(\ell\). Choose an actual lattice point
\[
a_0\in\ell\cap\mathbb Z^2.
\tag{33}
\]
Since \(u=(u_1,u_2)\) is primitive, there are \(p,q\in\mathbb Z\) such that
\(pu_1+qu_2=1\). If \(z\in\ell\cap\mathbb Z^2\), write
\(z-a_0=tu\). Then
\[
t=p(z_1-a_{0,1})+q(z_2-a_{0,2})\in\mathbb Z.
\]
Conversely \(a_0+ku\in\ell\cap\mathbb Z^2\) for every \(k\in\mathbb Z\).
Hence
\[
\ell\cap\mathbb Z^2=a_0+\mathbb Zu.
\tag{34}
\]

Compactness of \(C\) makes
\[
I:=\{k\in\mathbb Z:w_{a_0+ku}>0\}
\]
finite, and \(L_\ell>0\) makes it nonempty. It is a consecutive interval.
Indeed, accepted fact `4e868f774de77608` defines on the continuous base
projection the nonnegative concave function
\[
\rho(z):=M(z)^{1/d},
\tag{35}
\]
where \(M(z)=0\) on every zero-volume fiber. If \(k_0<k_1\) belong to
\(I\), then (9) makes \(\rho(a_0+k_i u)>0\) for \(i=0,1\). Concavity makes
\(\rho\) positive at every intermediate point of the segment, so every
intermediate integer fiber has positive volume. Thus
\[
I=\{k_-,k_-+1,\ldots,k_+\}.
\tag{36}
\]
By the zero convention for \(M_z\),
\[
\sum_{z\in\ell\cap\mathbb Z^2}M_z
=\sum_{k=k_-}^{k_+}M_{a_0+ku}.
\tag{37}
\]

Choose \(k_*\in I\) maximizing \(\rho(a_0+ku)\) over \(I\). Consider the
two sequences
\[
\rho(a_0+k_*u),\rho(a_0+(k_*+1)u),\ldots,
\rho(a_0+k_+u)
\tag{38}
\]
and
\[
\rho(a_0+k_*u),\rho(a_0+(k_*-1)u),\ldots,
\rho(a_0+k_-u).
\tag{39}
\]
Each is nonnegative, nonincreasing, and has nondecreasing drops. To see
this, concavity of \(\rho\) makes successive forward slopes
nonincreasing in either orientation, while maximality at the initial
integer point makes the first slope nonpositive. Let the sums of the
\(d\)-th powers in (38) and (39) be \(\Sigma_+\) and \(\Sigma_-\),
respectively. The maximizing term is counted twice, so
\[
\max\{\Sigma_+,\Sigma_-\}
\geq
\frac12\sum_{k=k_-}^{k_+}M_{a_0+ku}.
\tag{40}
\]

Choose a side \(\sigma\in\{-1,1\}\) attaining the maximum in (40), and
apply the sequence lemma to that side. It returns an index \(j\), with
\(j=0\) allowed, whose chord sum \(B_j\) satisfies
\[
B_j\geq\frac38\max\{\Sigma_+,\Sigma_-\}.
\tag{41}
\]
The initial term is positive by (9), so this application is not in the
all-zero case.

If \(j=0\), take
\[
E:=\{a_0+k_*u\}
\]
and choose \(x_0\in C_{a_0+k_*u}\) with
\(\delta_{a_0+k_*u}(x_0)=M_{a_0+k_*u}\); define \(s(a_0+k_*u):=x_0\).
If \(j\geq1\), take
\[
E:=\{a_0+k_*u,\ a_0+(k_*+\sigma j)u\},
\tag{42}
\]
choose depth maximizers \(x_0,x_j\) in the two endpoint fibers, and let
\(s\) be their affine interpolant. By (34), when \(j\geq1\) the lattice
points of the segment in (42) are exactly
\[
a_0+(k_*+\sigma k)u,\qquad 0\leq k\leq j.
\tag{43}
\]
For each such \(k\), joint concavity of the fiber-depth root from accepted
fact `4e868f774de77608` gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
&\delta_{a_0+(k_*+\sigma k)u}
\left(
\left(1-\frac{k}{j}\right)x_0+\frac{k}{j}x_j
\right)^{1/d}\\
&\qquad\geq
\left(1-\frac{k}{j}\right)
M_{a_0+k_*u}^{1/d}
+\frac{k}{j}M_{a_0+(k_*+\sigma j)u}^{1/d}.
\end{aligned}
\tag{44}
\]
Convexity of \(C\) also shows directly that every interpolated point in
(44) lies in its stated fiber. Raising (44) to the \(d\)-th power and
summing proves, for \(j\geq1\),
\[
\sum_{z\in\operatorname{conv}(E)\cap\mathbb Z^2}\delta_z(s(z))
\geq B_j.
\tag{45}
\]
For \(j=0\), equation (45) holds as well because both sides equal
\(M_{a_0+k_*u}\).

In both ranks \(2^{-q(E)}\geq1/2\). Combining (37), (40), (41), and (45)
gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
2^{-q(E)}
\sum_{z\in\operatorname{conv}(E)\cap\mathbb Z^2}\delta_z(s(z))
&\geq\frac12 B_j\\
&\geq\frac3{16}\max\{\Sigma_+,\Sigma_-\}\\
&\geq\frac3{32}
\sum_{z\in\ell\cap\mathbb Z^2}M_z.
\end{aligned}
\tag{46}
\]
Summing (9) over the positive-volume fibers on \(\ell\) gives
\[
\sum_{z\in\ell\cap\mathbb Z^2}M_z
\geq\frac1e\sum_{z\in\ell\cap\mathbb Z^2}w_z
=\frac{L_\ell}{e}.
\tag{47}
\]
Equations (46) and (47) prove (6).

It remains to prove the consequence for actual ambient mixed depth. Assume
(7), and put
\[
\Delta_E:=
\sum_{z\in\operatorname{conv}(E)\cap\mathbb Z^2}\delta_z(s(z)).
\tag{48}
\]
Equations (6) and (7) give
\[
2^{-q(E)}\Delta_E
\geq\frac{3L_\ell}{32e}
\geq\frac{W}{64}.
\tag{49}
\]
Since \(L_\ell>0\), one has \(W>0\).

First suppose \(q(E)=0\), so \(E=\{z^*\}\) and
\(\Delta_E=\delta_{z^*}(s(z^*))\). Let \(H\) be any closed ambient
halfspace containing \((z^*,s(z^*))\). If the fiber component of a normal
of \(H\) is nonzero, then the section of \(H\) over \(z^*\) is a proper
closed halfspace of \(\mathbb R^d\) containing \(s(z^*)\), and its
\(C_{z^*}\)-volume is at least \(\Delta_E\). If the fiber component is zero,
then membership in \(H\) is constant on the fiber over \(z^*\); since the
selected point belongs to \(H\), that entire fiber belongs to \(H\), and
its volume is \(w_{z^*}\geq\Delta_E\). The latter inequality holds because
some proper closed halfspace contains the compact fiber \(C_{z^*}\), so
the infimum defining \(\Delta_E\) is at most \(w_{z^*}\). This also covers
the whole-space halfspace. All other fiber contributions are nonnegative.
Hence
\[
\mathcal H_d\!\left(
C\cap(\mathbb Z^2\times\mathbb R^d)\cap H
\right)
\geq\Delta_E
\geq\frac{W}{64},
\tag{50}
\]
where the last inequality uses \(q(E)=0\) in (49). Thus rank zero is
handled directly, without applying a positive-base-dimension theorem.

Now suppose \(q(E)=1\). Order the endpoints as
\[
z^{(0)}=a_0+k_*u,\qquad
z^{(1)}=z^{(0)}+\sigma j u,
\qquad j\geq1,
\]
and define
\[
\widetilde C:=
\left\{
(t,x)\in[0,j]\times\mathbb R^d:
(z^{(0)}+\sigma t u,x)\in C
\right\}.
\tag{51}
\]
This is a compact convex set. Both endpoint fibers have positive
\(d\)-volume, hence contain open \(d\)-balls. The convex hull of those two
balls placed at base coordinates \(0\) and \(j\) has nonempty interior in
\(\mathbb R^{1+d}\) and is contained in \(\widetilde C\). Therefore
\(\widetilde C\) is a convex body in \(\mathbb R^{1+d}\).

The affine map
\[
\Phi:\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^d
\longrightarrow
\operatorname{aff}(E)\times\mathbb R^d,
\qquad
\Phi(t,x):=(z^{(0)}+\sigma t u,x)
\tag{52}
\]
identifies the mixed lattice exactly:
\[
\Phi(\mathbb Z\times\mathbb R^d)
=
\bigl(\operatorname{aff}(E)\cap\mathbb Z^2\bigr)\times\mathbb R^d.
\tag{53}
\]
Indeed, (53) is precisely the primitive-lattice identity (34), translated
to \(z^{(0)}\) and with \(u\) replaced by \(\sigma u\).

Define the affine selector on the one-dimensional base of
\(\widetilde C\) by
\[
q(t):=
\left(1-\frac{t}{j}\right)x_0+\frac{t}{j}x_j.
\tag{54}
\]
Convexity of \(C\) gives \((t,q(t))\in\widetilde C\) for every
\(t\in[0,j]\), so \(q\) is feasible on every positive-volume integer
fiber of \(\widetilde C\). The fiber at an integer \(t\in[0,j]\) is
exactly \(C_{z^{(0)}+\sigma t u}\), and its selector depth is exactly
\(\delta_{z^{(0)}+\sigma t u}(s(z^{(0)}+\sigma t u))\). Hence the sum of
the selector depths for \(\widetilde C\) is \(\Delta_E\). Equation (49)
shows that \(\Delta_E>0\).

Apply accepted fact `b220933817d23295` to \(\widetilde C\) with base
dimension one and selector (54). It gives an integer
\(t^*\in\{0,\ldots,j\}\) such that
\[
\widetilde y^*:=(t^*,q(t^*))
\]
has mixed halfspace depth in \(\widetilde C\) at least
\[
\frac12\Delta_E
=2^{-q(E)}\Delta_E
\geq\frac{W}{64}.
\tag{55}
\]
This is the only use of accepted fact `b220933817d23295`.

Set \(y^*:=\Phi(\widetilde y^*)\). Let \(H\) be any closed halfspace in
\(\mathbb R^{2+d}\) containing \(y^*\). Its preimage
\[
\widetilde H:=\Phi^{-1}(H)
\tag{56}
\]
is a closed halfspace in \(\mathbb R^{1+d}\), possibly the whole space,
and it contains \(\widetilde y^*\). Under (52), the \(d\)-dimensional
measure in every corresponding fiber is unchanged. Therefore, using only
nonnegative contributions from the original fibers omitted by (51),
\[
\begin{aligned}
&\mathcal H_d\!\left(
C\cap(\mathbb Z^2\times\mathbb R^d)\cap H
\right)\\
&\qquad\geq
\sum_{t\in\mathbb Z}
\operatorname{vol}_d\!\left(
\widetilde C_t\cap(\widetilde H)_t
\right)
\geq\frac{W}{64}.
\end{aligned}
\tag{57}
\]
The final inequality is (55). Because \(H\) was arbitrary, (57) transfers
the restricted rank-one depth monotonically to the original ambient body.
All halfspaces used above are closed, so boundary mass is retained. This
proves the consequence and completes the lemma.
statement:
Let \(d\in\mathbb Z_{>0}\), let
\(C\subseteq\mathbb R^2\times\mathbb R^d\) be a convex body, and write
\[
C_z:=\{x\in\mathbb R^d:(z,x)\in C\},\qquad
w_z:=\operatorname{vol}_d(C_z),\qquad
W:=\sum_{z\in\mathbb Z^2}w_z.
\tag{1}
\]
For \(w_z>0\) and \(x\in C_z\), put
\[
\delta_z(x):=
\inf\left\{
\operatorname{vol}_d(C_z\cap J):
J\subseteq\mathbb R^d
\text{ is a proper closed halfspace and }x\in J
\right\},
\tag{2}
\]
and define
\[
M_z:=\max_{x\in C_z}\delta_z(x).
\tag{3}
\]
For every empty or zero-volume lattice fiber, define \(M_z:=0\).

Let \(u\in\mathbb Z^2\) be primitive, let \(\ell\) be an affine line
parallel to \(u\) with \(\ell\cap\mathbb Z^2\ne\varnothing\), and put
\[
L_\ell:=\sum_{z\in\ell\cap\mathbb Z^2}w_z.
\tag{4}
\]
If \(L_\ell>0\), there are one or two positive-fiber lattice points
\[
E\subseteq\ell\cap\mathbb Z^2,
\qquad
q(E):=\dim\operatorname{aff}(E)\in\{0,1\},
\tag{5}
\]
fiber-depth maximizers at the points of \(E\), and their affine interpolant
\(s\), such that
\[
2^{-q(E)}
\sum_{z\in\operatorname{conv}(E)\cap\mathbb Z^2}
\delta_z(s(z))
\geq
\frac3{32}\sum_{z\in\ell\cap\mathbb Z^2}M_z
\geq
\frac{3L_\ell}{32e}.
\tag{6}
\]
In rank zero the sum in (6) is the single fiber depth. Consequently, if
\[
L_\ell\geq\frac{eW}{6},
\tag{7}
\]
then \(C\cap(\mathbb Z^2\times\mathbb R^d)\) has a point of mixed
halfspace depth at least \(W/64\).
